paras: The reported flaying of a Black man in Craven County, North Carolina, was a story carried by Southern newspapers in late May and early June 1888 that a man described as 'a negro' had been skinned alive by the friends of a young woman teacher he was accused of assaulting. According to the story he died a few minutes after the flaying, which was done at the teacher's request. The account traced to a single source, J. T. Winfield of Craven County, and the Washington Gazette, which first printed it, called it a rumor whose truth was 'not vouched for.'

As told, a young woman teacher was taken by a man, carried into the woods, bound hand and foot and assaulted. He then tied her to a tree and left, saying he would return to kill her. Friends who missed her searched the country in large numbers, found her and cut her loose, then asked her to stay in place while they hid in the bushes.

When the man came back, a dozen guns were leveled at him and he surrendered. Asked to name his fate, the teacher said she wished him flayed alive, and he was flayed, 'living but a few minutes afterward.' The Atlanta Constitution added that his friends were told what had happened and took his body.
None of the reports names the dead man, the teacher, the place or the date, and no report of an inquest, arrest or official inquiry appears in the coverage.

The story reached the press through a Raleigh telegram of May 26, which the Richmond Dispatch printed under 'Horrible Crime and Fearful Punishment' and closed with 'Such is the story told by Mr. J. T. Winfield, of Craven county.' The Atlanta Constitution ran a fuller Raleigh special as 'Flayed Alive: The Terrible Punishment Meted Out to a Negro Brute,' presenting it without qualification. The Charlotte Democrat reprinted the Dispatch item in its 'State News' column on June 1.

Closer to the source, the Washington Gazette's version, reprinted from the Wilson Mirror by the Durham Recorder on June 6, said Winfield had related what 'rumor' reported and that the story was unverified though 'plausible.' That paper likened the affair to Shakespeare's 'Rape of Lucrece', while the Shenandoah Herald, through the Raleigh correspondent of the Whig, headed it 'Skinned Alive.' Across these papers the accused was called 'the brute', 'the wretch' and 'the fiend', and the killing was described as punishment rather than crime.

Details varied in retelling: most versions say the teacher was carried into the woods and bound, while the Shenandoah Herald says she was overtaken while walking, bound and gagged, and that 'several men' waited for the man's return. The papers also differed on how firm the report was, since the Raleigh telegrams gave it as news while the Gazette version called it rumor.

reader.title: Reported flaying of a Black man in Craven County, North Carolina (1888)
bases: The reports describe a man accused of assaulting a teacher who was captured by her armed friends and flayed to death at her request, with no legal process (A2, A3, A5).

As told, the account meets every part of the definition: a dozen armed men captured the accused and killed him by flaying as punishment for an alleged assault (A2, A3). But every version traces to one secondhand rumor, related by J. T. Winfield to the Washington Gazette, which said the report was 'not vouched for'; no victim, teacher, place or date is named and no confirmation was found (A5, A6).

The four texts that carry the story all derive from Winfield's account as published by the Washington Gazette, which presented it as rumor; no independent report confirms or denies it (A2, A3, A5, A6).

accounts.label: Raleigh telegram (Richmond Dispatch and Atlanta Constitution)
accounts.gist: Reported as news received in Raleigh on May 26, without qualification, attributed to J. T. Winfield in the Dispatch; the Constitution adds that his friends got his body.

accounts.label: Washington Gazette via Wilson Mirror
accounts.gist: The same story told to a Gazette reporter by Winfield, explicitly as rumor 'not vouched for' though 'plausible'.

accounts.label: Raleigh correspondent of the Whig
accounts.gist: Gazette version with variant details: overtaken while walking, gagged; 'several men' waited; she replied 'Skin him alive'.

framing.detail: The Atlanta Constitution headlined it 'Flayed Alive: The Terrible Punishment Meted Out to a Negro Brute' and called him 'the wretch'.
The Richmond Dispatch ran it as 'Horrible Crime and Fearful Punishment' in a Raleigh news column, calling the man 'the brute' and the punishment 'terrible'.
The Wilson Mirror version, reprinted in Durham, called it 'A Horrible Horror', flagged it as unverified rumor and likened it to Shakespeare's 'Rape of Lucrece'.
